lead: Unix and Linux are related by design, not by shared source code. Unix began in 1969 at Bell Labs as a small multiuser system. It was rewritten in C in 1973, which made it easier to move to new computers. Different groups then built BSD and System V, and POSIX later set a common interface. Linux is a free Unix-like kernel (the core program of an operating system) that Linus Torvalds started in 1991. With GNU tools, it became a complete system used on servers, Android phones, cloud machines and routers. The timeline and the design ideas that survived explain today's command line.
prereq: You need: no earlier chapter; this is the first chapter.

blocks.text: Unix began at Bell Labs in 1969. The usual names are Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie. They wanted a small multiuser operating system for a spare DEC computer. Multiuser means many people can log in at once. Multitasking means many programs can run at once. The first version was written in assembly language, which ties code to one machine.

In 1973 the team rewrote Unix in C. C is a portable systems programming language. A C compiler can be built for many processors, so the same source can be rebuilt on a new computer. This rewrite helped Unix spread to universities and companies.

Two families became important: BSD from Berkeley and System V from AT&T. They shared ideas but differed in system calls and tools. A program written for one might not build on the other. POSIX addressed this by defining a standard set of interfaces. POSIX is not an operating system; it is a written standard. A program that uses only POSIX calls can be built on many Unix-like systems.

The kernel is the core program that manages memory, processes and devices. The shell is an ordinary user program that reads commands and asks the kernel to act. Their split is covered in Kernel, shell and user space.

Minix was a small Unix-like teaching system. It gave students source code to read, but it was not a full production kernel. Linus Torvalds, then a student in Finland, began a kernel for his own PC. In 1991 he announced the project; the first public version was small. He chose the GNU General Public License, or GPL. The GPL is a copyright licence that lets anyone run, study, change and redistribute the code, provided derived code keeps the same licence. This is one form of open source; see Open source software and its benefits.

Linux is the kernel, not the whole system. A usable system also needs libraries, compilers, a shell and commands. Much of that came from the GNU project, which had built free tools but lacked a working kernel. The combination is often called GNU/Linux. Linux 1.0 appeared in 1994. Later, distributions packaged the kernel with tools and an installer; see Linux distributions and installation. Features such as multi-user login and loadable modules are covered in Linux features.

Because the source was free, many people could fix bugs and port the kernel to new machines. That is why Linux reached servers, phones and embedded boards. Android, for example, uses a Linux kernel. The kernel is not Unix source code; it is an independent Unix-like kernel.

Unix and Linux share a style of design. Small tools do one job well. A tool reads text, writes text, and exits. The shell connects tools with pipes, so the output of one becomes the input of the next. The shell is a program that reads commands and starts other programs. This is why text streams matter: a log file, a CSV file or a command output can all be processed by the same filters.

The phrase everything is a file is a shorthand. In Unix-like systems, many resources are reached through file operations: open, read, write, close. A device, a pipe or a network socket can be used through a file descriptor, which is a small integer that names an open file. This does not mean every object is a regular file on disk; it means the same interface is reused. Unit 2 covers files and permissions; Unit 3 covers pipes and filters.

Portable C is another pillar. The kernel and tools are mostly written in C. When C is available on a new CPU, much of the software can be rebuilt with few changes. The shell is also portable: a script written for a POSIX shell can run on many systems. The command line is that text loop; see Command-line interface and basic commands.

These ideas are not laws. They are conventions that make systems easy to combine. A small tool can be tested alone. A text stream can be inspected by eye. A file interface can be reused by many programs. That is the practical legacy of Unix, and Linux carries it forward.

examples.question: Arrange these four events in time order and give the gap in years between the first and last: Linux 1.0 (1994), Unix work begins (1969), Linux kernel announced (1991), Unix rewritten in C (1973).
steps: Read each event with its year: Unix work begins = 1969; Unix rewritten in C = 1973; Linux kernel announced = 1991; Linux 1.0 = 1994.
Sort by year in ascending order: 1969 Unix work begins, 1973 Unix rewritten in C, 1991 Linux kernel announced, 1994 Linux 1.0.
Gap = last year − first year = 1994 − 1969 = 25 years.
examples.answer: The order is Unix work begins (1969), Unix rewritten in C (1973), Linux kernel announced (1991), Linux 1.0 (1994); the gap is 25 years.
examples.check:
events = [
    ("Unix work begins", 1969),
    ("Unix rewritten in C", 1973),
    ("Linux kernel announced", 1991),
    ("Linux 1.0", 1994),
]
events.sort(key=lambda item: item[1])
for name, year in events:
    print(year)
print(events[-1][1] - events[0][1])

traps: Linux is not a version of Unix source code; it is an independently written Unix-like kernel.
BSD and System V are Unix branches, not Linux distributions. A Linux distribution packages the Linux kernel with tools.
POSIX is an interface standard, not an operating system or a kernel.
The GPL is a software licence; it does not mean the code has no owner.
The key dates are 1969 for Unix work, 1973 for the C rewrite, 1991 for the Linux kernel announcement and 1994 for Linux 1.0; do not swap them.

quiz.q: In which year did Unix work begin at Bell Labs, and in which year was Unix rewritten in C?
quiz.a: Unix work began in 1969; Unix was rewritten in C in 1973.

quiz.q: Who started the Linux kernel, and in which year was it announced?
quiz.a: Linus Torvalds started it; the project was announced in 1991.

quiz.q: Why did the C rewrite help Unix spread to new machines?
quiz.a: C compilers can be built for many processors, so the same source can be rebuilt with fewer changes than assembly code. This reduced the work needed for each new machine.
BSD and System V differed in their interfaces. POSIX defined a common set of system calls and interfaces so a program using only POSIX calls could be built on many Unix-like systems.

quiz.q: A course lists Unix work beginning in 1969 and Linux 1.0 in 1994. How many years apart are they? If a student says Linux came 10 years after Unix, by how many years is that wrong?
quiz.a: Gap = 1994 − 1969 = 25 years. The student's claim is wrong by 25 − 10 = 15 years.

quiz.q: A student says 'Linux is Unix because the commands look the same.' Give two corrections.
quiz.a: The Linux kernel is independently written and does not use Unix source code. The similar commands come from Unix-like design and from GNU tools, not from Linux being a Unix version.

quiz.q: Why can a program that uses only POSIX calls run on both a BSD system and Linux, while a program using a vendor-specific call may not?
quiz.a: POSIX calls are a common standard found on both systems. A vendor-specific call exists on one system only, so the program depends on that system and cannot be moved without a rewrite.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Linux runs most public cloud servers and Android phones, and containers share the same kernel. Researchers study schedulers, file systems and security in the Linux kernel because the source is open. New curricula often add containers and cloud early, but the Unix timeline still explains why commands look the way they do. Search for 'Unix history Bell Labs', 'Linux kernel archive' and 'POSIX standard' to go deeper.
